exampleAnswers.title: Identifying the Formula For Negating a Quantified Statement

question.explanation:
To negate the existential statement $\exists m \in X, \, \neg C(m),$ we flip the quantifier to universal and negate the predicate:

\begin{align*} \neg \left( \exists m \in X, \, \neg C(m) \right) &\equiv \forall m \in X, \,\neg\neg C(m) \\[5pt] &\equiv \forall m \in \bbox[2pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue}X}, \, \bbox[2pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue} C(m)} \end{align*}

question.explanation:
To negate the universal statement $\forall y \in \overline{K}, \, \neg R(y),$ we flip the quantifier to existential and negate the predicate:

\begin{align*} \neg \left( \forall y \in \overline{K}, \, \neg R(y) \right) &\equiv \exists y \in \overline{K}, \,\neg\neg R(y) \\[5pt] &\equiv \bbox[3pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\exists} y \in \overline{K}, \, \bbox[2pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue}R(y)} \end{align*}

example.title: Identifying the Formula For Negating a Quantified Statement

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ For all $n \in \mathbb{N},$ $n^2$ is not prime.
question.choice1: There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n^2$ is prime.
question.choice2: There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n^2$ is not prime.
question.explanation:
If we denote

\[ P(n): \textrm{$n^2$ is prime}, \]

our statement can be written as

\[ \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n). \]

Negating this, we obtain

\begin{align*} \neg \left( \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n) \right) &\equiv \exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg\neg P(n) \\[3pt] &\equiv \exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \ P(n). \end{align*}

Finally, $\exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n)$ reads as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n^2$ is prime.

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ For all $q \in \mathbb{Z},$ $q^2$ is even.
question.choice1: There exists $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $q^2$ is not even.
question.choice2: There exists $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $q^2$ is even.
question.explanation:
If we denote

\[ P(q): \textrm{$q^2$ is even}, \]

our statement can be written as

\[ \forall q \in \mathbb{Z}, \, P(q). \]

Negating this, we obtain

\begin{align*} \neg \left( \forall q \in \mathbb{Z}, \, P(q) \right) &\equiv \exists q \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \ \neg P(q). \end{align*}

Finally, $\exists q \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \neg P(q)$ reads as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $q^2$ is not even.

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ All triangles are not acute.
question.explanation:
Let $T$ be the set of all triangles. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ For all $x \in T,$ $x$ is not acute.

Introducing the universal quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\forall x \in T, \, \textrm{$x$ is not acute}.$

Negating this, we obtain \begin{align*} \neg \left( \forall x \in T, \, \textrm{$x$ is not acute} \right) &\equiv \exists x \in T, \, \neg \big( \textrm{$x$ is not acute} \big) \\[5pt] &\equiv \exists x \in T, \, \textrm{$x$ is acute} \end{align*}

which reads

$\qquad$ There exists $x \in T$ such that $x$ is acute.

or simply

$\qquad$ Some triangles are acute.

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ Every sequence is arithmetic.
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be the set of all sequences. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ For all $s\in S,$ $s$ is arithmetic.

Introducing the universal quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\forall s \in S, \, \textrm{$s$ is arithmetic}.$

Negating this, we obtain

\begin{align*} \neg \left( \forall s \in S, \, \textrm{$s$ is arithmetic} \right) &\equiv \exists s \in S, \, \neg \big( \textrm{$s$ is arithmetic} \big) \\[5pt] &\equiv \exists s \in S, \, \textrm{$s$ is not arithmetic} \end{align*}

which reads

$\qquad$ There exists $s \in S$ such that $s$ is not arithmetic.

or simply

$\qquad$ Some sequences are not arithmetic.

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ Every real $2\times 2$ matrix is not singular.
question.choice2: Some real $2\times 2$ matrices are not singular.
question.choice4: Every real $2\times 2$ matrix is not singular.
question.explanation:
Let $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ be the set of all real $2\times 2$ matrices. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ For all $x \in M_2(\mathbb{R}),$ $x$ is not singular.

Introducing the universal quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\forall x \in M_2(\mathbb{R}), \, \textrm{$x$ is not singular}.$

Negating this, we obtain \begin{align*} \neg \left( \forall x \in M_2(\mathbb{R}), \, \textrm{$x$ is not singular} \right) &\equiv \exists x \in M_2(\mathbb{R}), \, \neg \big( \textrm{$x$ is not singular} \big) \\[5pt] &\equiv \exists x \in M_2(\mathbb{R}), \, \textrm{$x$ is singular} \end{align*}

which reads

$\qquad$ There exists $x \in M_2(\mathbb{R})$ such that $x$ is singular.

or simply

$\qquad$ Some real $2\times 2$ matrices are singular.

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ Some rational numbers are not proper fractions.
question.choice1: All rational numbers are proper fractions.
question.choice2: All rational numbers are not proper fractions.
question.choice3: Some rational numbers are not proper fractions.
question.choice4: Some rational numbers are proper fractions.
question.explanation:
The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $x \in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $x$ is not a proper fraction.

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\exists x \in \mathbb{Q}, \, x \textrm{ is not a proper fraction}.$

Negating this, we obtain

\begin{align*} \neg \left( \exists x \in \mathbb{Q}, \, x \textrm{ is not a proper fraction} \right) &\equiv \forall x \in \mathbb{Q}, \, \neg \big( x \textrm{ is not a proper fraction} \big) \\[3pt] &\equiv \forall x \in \mathbb{Q}, \, x \textrm{ is a proper fraction} \end{align*}

which reads

$\qquad$ For all $x \in \mathbb{Q},$ $x \textrm{ is a proper fraction}.$

or simply

$\qquad$ All rational numbers are proper fractions.

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\dfrac{n}{10} \in \mathbb{N}.$
question.explanation:
If we denote \[ P(n): \dfrac{n}{10} \in \mathbb{N} , \]

our statement can be written as \[ \exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n). \]

Negating this, we obtain \[ \neg \left( \exists n \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n) \right) \equiv \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n). \]

Finally, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \, \neg P(n)$ reads as follows:

$\qquad$ For all $n \in \mathbb{N},$ $\dfrac{n}{10} \boldsymbol{\not\in} \mathbb{N}.$

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ There exists $x \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $x^2$ is not positive.
question.choice3: There exists $x \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $x^2$ is not positive.
question.choice4: There exists $x \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $x^2$ is positive.
question.explanation:
If we denote \[ P(x): \textrm{$x^2$ is positive}, \]

our statement can be written as \[ \exists x \in \mathbb{C}, \, \neg P(x). \]

Negating this, we obtain \begin{align*} \neg \left( \exists x \in \mathbb{C}, \, \neg P(x) \right) &\equiv \forall x \in \mathbb{C}, \,\neg\neg P(x) \\[5pt] &\equiv \forall x \in \mathbb{C}, \, P(x). \end{align*}

Finally, $\forall x \in \mathbb{C}, \, P(x)$ reads as follows:

$\qquad$ For all $x \in \mathbb{C},$ $x^2$ is positive.

$\qquad$ There exists $n\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $2n$ is not composite.
question.choice3: There exists $n\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $2n$ is not composite.
question.choice4: There exists $n\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $2n$ is composite.
question.explanation:
If we denote \[ P(n): \textrm{$2n$ is composite}, \]

Finally, $\forall n\in \mathbb{N}, \, P(n)$ reads as follows:

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ At least one existential statement is not true.
question.choice2: Every existential statement is not true.
question.choice3: At least one existential statement is true.
question.choice4: At least one existential statement is not true.
question.explanation:
Let $E$ be the set of all existential statements. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $S \in E$ such that $S$ is not true.

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\exists S \in E, \, \textrm{$S$ is not true}.$

Negating this, we obtain \begin{align*} \neg \left( \exists S \in E, \, \textrm{$S$ is not true} \right) &\equiv \forall S\in E, \, \neg \big( \textrm{$S$ is not true} \big) \\[3pt] &\equiv \forall S \in E, \, \textrm{$S$ is true} \end{align*}

which reads

$\qquad$ For all $S\in E,$ $S$ is true.

or simply

$\qquad$ Every existential statement is true.
